cards.front: Which receptor does histamine use to switch on acid secretion by the parietal cell, and what does it do?
cards.back: H2 receptors on the basolateral membrane. Activation raises cAMP, which switches on the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump, the final step of acid secretion. Histamine is the dominant physiological stimulus; gastrin and acetylcholine act partly by releasing histamine from ECL cells.

cards.front: What imbalance is thought to cause peptic ulcer, and how does acid fit in gastric versus duodenal ulcer?
cards.back: Ulcer arises when aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, bile, H. pylori) outweigh defensive ones (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, NO, mucosal blood flow). Gastric ulcer: acid is normal or low and weak defence matters more. Duodenal ulcer: acid is high in about half. Acid is still an aggressive factor either way, so lowering it is the main treatment.

cards.front: Which stimuli and receptors drive the parietal cell, and which second messengers do they use?
cards.back: Histamine (H2, via cAMP), acetylcholine (M3) and gastrin (CCK2) act on the basolateral membrane to switch on the apical H+/K+ ATPase. Muscarinic and gastrin receptors work through PLC-IP3-DAG and raised Ca2+. Gastrin comes from antral G cells; vagal ACh and GRP drive its release, with M1 receptors on enteric ganglion cells.

cards.front: How do prostaglandins protect the gastric mucosa?
cards.back: Prostaglandins from the mucosa lower acid output and raise mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow. The mucus-bicarbonate gel keeps H+ and pepsin off the epithelium.

cards.front: Why do H2 blockers also reduce acid responses to gastrin and acetylcholine?
cards.back: Histamine plays a permissive role. The cAMP made by H2 activation is needed for a full secretory response to gastrin and cholinergic agonists, so H2 blockade weakens the response to almost every secretagogue.

cards.front: Compare cimetidine, ranitidine and famotidine on potency and antiandrogen effects.
cards.back: Ranitidine is about 5 times as potent as cimetidine, and famotidine about 5 to 8 times as potent as ranitidine. Only cimetidine has antiandrogenic effects (gynaecomastia, loss of libido), raises prolactin and slows hepatic breakdown of estradiol. GG14 notes that some ranitidine and nizatidine preparations have been withdrawn because of contamination.

cards.front: Why can cimetidine cause so many drug interactions and endocrine effects, and how do ranitidine and famotidine differ?
cards.back: Cimetidine inhibits several CYP450 isoenzymes and cuts hepatic blood flow, so drugs such as theophylline, phenytoin, warfarin and lidocaine accumulate. It also blocks androgen receptors and raises prolactin (gynaecomastia, impotence). Ranitidine and famotidine lack these actions. Antacids reduce H2 blocker absorption, so separate by 2 h.

cards.front: Why have PPIs replaced H2 blockers for ulcer healing, and where do H2 blockers still have a role?
cards.back: PPIs heal ulcers faster with better pain relief and a higher healing rate, even in NSAID ulcers and H. pylori ulcers. H2 blockers still have a role in stress-ulcer bleeding prophylaxis (i.v.). For ulcer healing a single bedtime dose works as well as split doses because nocturnal acid is the target.

cards.front: Essay: Targets of acid-peptic drugs, from the parietal cell to the mucosa

points: Acid, pepsin, bile, H. pylori versus mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, blood flow
Aim of therapy: pain relief, healing, preventing complications and relapse
Histamine (H2, cAMP) dominant; ACh (M3) and gastrin (CCK2) use IP3-Ca2+ and also release histamine from ECL cells
H+/K+ ATPase is the final common step
H2 blockers: block histamine and, through its permissive role, other stimuli; mainly nocturnal acid
PPIs: irreversibly inhibit the proton pump, 80-98 percent suppression at steady state
Anticholinergics and pirenzepine (M1): obsolete because of side effects
Misoprostol: PGE1 analogue; ulcer protectives sucralfate and bismuth; antacids neutralise
PPI first for ulcer, NSAID ulcer, GERD and Zollinger-Ellison
H2 blockers for milder or intermittent disease; antacids for quick symptom relief
H. pylori positive ulcers need a PPI plus antibiotics
Rebound hypergastrinaemia and long-term PPI concerns; misoprostol diarrhoea and abortion; cimetidine interactions

cards.front: Mechanism: omeprazole
cards.text: Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits the {{H+/K+ ATPase}} proton pump, and it is converted to its reactive form only in the acidic {{canaliculus}} of the parietal cell.

cards.front: Why are PPIs swallowed whole and taken before a meal?
cards.back: They are acid labile, so they are given as enteric-coated forms that must not be crushed or chewed. Taken on an empty stomach, the drug is in the blood when a meal switches the pumps on, and food lowers bioavailability.

cards.front: List the PPIs in KDT and the one distinguishing point of each.
cards.back: Omeprazole (prototype; inhibits CYP2C19); esomeprazole (S-enantiomer, longer t1/2); lansoprazole (partly reversible binding); pantoprazole (acid stable, i.v. for bleeding, fewest interactions); rabeprazole (faster onset, higher pKa); ilaprazole (about twice as potent as omeprazole). S-pantoprazole and dexrabeprazole are the active single isomers, giving the same effect at about half the dose.

cards.front: Why does a PPI take 3 to 4 days to reach full acid suppression?
cards.back: Each dose blocks only the pumps that are actively secreting, and the drug is cleared within 1 to 2 hours. Repeated dosing blocks more pumps until a plateau is reached at about 3 to 4 days, with 80 to 98 percent of 24-hour acid output suppressed. Secretion takes 3 to 4 days to return after stopping.

cards.front: What are the main concerns with long-term high-dose PPI therapy?
cards.back: Compensatory hypergastrinaemia with ECL-cell hyperplasia, fundic gland polyps and atrophic gastritis (tumour risk appears very low), and rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping. Loss of the acid barrier raises the risk of infections such as hospital-acquired pneumonia, community-acquired Clostridium difficile and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Reduced vitamin B12 absorption, hypomagnesaemia, and osteoporosis-related fractures are also reported, as are interstitial nephritis and, with omeprazole, gynaecomastia and erectile dysfunction.

cards.front: Why does omeprazole matter with clopidogrel, and which PPI has the fewest interactions?
cards.back: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, the enzyme that activates clopidogrel, which can blunt its antiplatelet effect. Omeprazole also raises levels of warfarin, diazepam and phenytoin. Pantoprazole has the lowest affinity for cytochrome P450 and the least interaction risk.

Benzimidazole derivatives given as enteric-coated forms

Acid returns only when new pump molecules are made (half-time about 18 hours)
Plasma half-life 1 to 2 hours, but acid suppression lasts 2 to 3 days
Food reduces absorption; take before a meal
Metabolised by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4; omeprazole needs no dose change in the elderly or in renal or hepatic impairment
Peptic, NSAID-induced and bleeding ulcers; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
GERD (drugs of choice), H. pylori eradication, stress ulcer prophylaxis
Mild: headache, loose stools, abdominal pain
Long-term: hypergastrinaemia, atrophic gastritis, infections, osteoporosis

cards.front: Which clinical situations call for a PPI as drug of choice, and how is dosing changed?
cards.back: Drug of choice for NSAID-induced ulcer (higher or twice-daily dose; healing occurs even if the NSAID continues), GERD (higher or twice-daily dose than for ulcer), Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (60-120 mg/day in 2 doses) and bleeding ulcer (high-dose i.v. PPI so acid does not dissolve the clot). It is also part of every H. pylori regimen, given twice daily to hold pH high.

cards.front: Essay: Proton pump inhibitors, pharmacology and safety

points: Class, prototype and site of action in the parietal cell
Why they have replaced H2 blockers as first-line acid suppressants
Activated only at low pH, then binds covalently to H+/K+ ATPase
Trapped in the canaliculus, so the action is confined to acid-secreting cells
Enteric-coated, taken before meals
Hepatic CYP metabolism creates interaction risk (CYP2C19 and CYP3A4)
Peptic, NSAID-induced and bleeding ulcers
GERD, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, H. pylori therapy, IV for stress ulcers

cards.front: How does sucralfate protect an ulcer without neutralising acid?
cards.back: Below pH 4 it polymerises into a sticky gel that binds to the ulcer base and forms a physical shield against acid, pepsin and bile. It has no acid-neutralising action and is barely absorbed. Antacids must not be given with it, because they stop it polymerising.

cards.front: What is colloidal bismuth subcitrate, and why is it not an antacid?
cards.back: A colloidal bismuth compound that heals ulcers without raising gastric pH. It precipitates below pH 5. Its benefit may come from protecting the ulcer base, raising mucosal prostaglandin, mucus and bicarbonate, and acting directly on H. pylori. It causes black tongue and stools, and milk or antacids must be avoided with it.

cards.front: Classify: ulcer protectives
cards.text: {{Sucralfate}} forms a protective gel below pH {{4}}, and {{misoprostol}} is a synthetic {{PGE1}} analogue that lowers acid output.

cards.front: Why is misoprostol seldom used for ulcers now?
cards.back: It is a synthetic PGE1 analogue that lowers acid output, but the effect lasts only about 3 hours, it relieves ulcer pain poorly, and it needs four times daily dosing. Diarrhoea, cramps and uterine bleeding are common, and it can cause abortion. Its main remaining role is preventing NSAID-induced ulcers.

cards.front: Why should every H. pylori-positive ulcer patient be offered eradication?
cards.back: Eradication is standard care in every H. pylori-positive gastric or duodenal ulcer: unless the patient keeps taking NSAIDs, it almost abolishes recurrence. H. pylori also drives chronic gastritis and contributes to gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric MALT lymphoma, which can regress after eradication. KDT adds that where testing is unavailable, failed or relapsing ulcers should still receive eradication therapy.

cards.front: Which H. pylori eradication regimens are listed in the textbooks?
cards.back: GG14 (newest): triple therapy for 10 to 14 days, a PPI twice daily with clarithromycin 500 mg and amoxicillin 1 g twice daily (metronidazole 500 mg can replace amoxicillin); bismuth quadruple therapy for 10 to 14 days, a PPI with bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole four times daily; sequential therapy (PPI + amoxicillin for 5 days, then PPI + clarithromycin + tinidazole or metronidazole for 5 days); or PPI + amoxicillin + levofloxacin for 10 days. Where resistance to clarithromycin and metronidazole is common, a 14-day quadruple regimen is advised. KDT cites the older US-FDA regimen: lansoprazole 30 mg + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg, all twice daily for 2 weeks (86 to 92 percent eradication).

cards.front: Short note: H. pylori eradication therapy

points: Heals ulcers and almost abolishes recurrence
Linked to gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma
A PPI raises gastric pH and enhances amoxicillin and clarithromycin activity
Amoxicillin, clarithromycin, metronidazole or tinidazole, tetracycline, levofloxacin
Bismuth: active against H. pylori and resistance does not develop to it
Single antibiotics fail and breed resistance; use two or three antibiotics with a PPI
10 to 14 days is better than shorter courses (GG14); KDT notes 1-week triple therapy gives about 85 percent
Resistance to clarithromycin and metronidazole is a major cause of failure; in tropical countries metronidazole resistance is commoner
Triple: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole) twice daily
Bismuth quadruple: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole for 10 to 14 days, used first where resistance is high and for treatment failures
Alternatives: sequential therapy; PPI + amoxicillin + levofloxacin
Recent nitroimidazole use: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin
Recent macrolide use: PPI + metronidazole or tinidazole + amoxicillin

cards.front: H. pylori regimen after a recent macrolide
cards.text: After recent macrolide use, the H. pylori regimen is a PPI with amoxicillin and {{metronidazole}} or {{tinidazole}}, and {{clarithromycin}} is left out.

cards.front: Essay: Drug management of peptic ulcer disease

points: Imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) and defensive factors (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins)
Pain relief, ulcer healing, prevention of bleeding and perforation, prevention of relapse
PPIs: first choice, faster and more complete healing
H2 blockers: alternative in uncomplicated cases, slower healing
Sucralfate, bismuth and misoprostol as protectives
Eradicate with a PPI plus two or three antibiotics for 10 to 14 days (triple or bismuth quadruple therapy)
Eradication almost abolishes relapse unless NSAIDs continue
NSAID ulcer: stop the NSAID if possible; PPIs heal and prevent NSAID ulcers better than H2 blockers or misoprostol
Bleeding ulcer: high-dose IV PPI, then oral PPI
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: PPI at about twice the usual dose

cards.front: Short note: Antacids

points: Basic salts that neutralise HCl; potency given as acid neutralising capacity
Do not reduce acid production; acid rebound follows
Act for 30 to 60 minutes on an empty stomach, 2 to 3 hours after meals
Sodium bicarbonate: fast but gives CO2 (distension), alkalosis and a sodium load
Sodium citrate: similar, but no CO2
Magnesium salts: laxative; accumulate in renal failure
Aluminium hydroxide: constipating, binds phosphate, toxicity in renal failure
Calcium carbonate: stimulates gastrin and rebound; milk-alkali syndrome
Fast plus slow acting components; laxative and constipating salts balance bowel effects
Reduce absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, iron and ketoconazole; separate doses by 2 hours

cards.front: Classify: antacid salts
cards.text: Magnesium hydroxide is {{fast-acting}} and laxative, aluminium hydroxide is {{slow-acting}} and {{constipating}}, so combining them balances the effect on the bowel.

cards.front: How is antacid potency expressed, and why do antacids give only short relief?
cards.back: Potency is the acid neutralising capacity: mEq of 1N HCl brought to pH 3.5 in a set time by a unit dose. A dose on an empty stomach acts only 30 to 60 min before emptying into the duodenum; with meals up to 2 to 3 h. Antacids do not reduce acid production.

cards.front: Why is sodium bicarbonate a poor routine antacid despite its quick action?
cards.back: It acts instantly but briefly, is absorbed (large doses cause alkalosis), releases CO2 (distension, belching, perforation risk in ulcer), gives a short acid rebound and adds a sodium load that can worsen oedema and heart failure. It is limited to casual heartburn, urine alkalinisation and acidosis.

cards.front: Short note: Drug therapy of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

points: Lower oesophageal sphincter tone is the main barrier
Fats, alcohol, smoking, anticholinergics, nitrates and calcium channel blockers lower LES tone
Acid is the key aggressive factor
Stage 1: occasional heartburn, no lesions: lifestyle, then on-demand antacid or H2 blocker
Stage 2 and 3: PPI, often twice daily, usually long term
PPI: most effective; heals 80 to 90 percent of lesions in 4 to 8 weeks
H2 blocker: mild disease; healing in 50 to 70 percent
Alginate: floating raft over gastric contents, no effect on LES
Prokinetics: adjuncts only, weaker than acid suppression
Light early dinner, raised head of bed, weight loss, avoid triggers

cards.front: Why are magnesium and aluminium salts combined, and what goes wrong with calcium carbonate?
cards.back: Magnesium salts act fast and are laxative and hasten emptying; aluminium hydroxide acts slowly, constipates and delays emptying, so the mixture balances bowel and emptying effects and allows lower doses, so less systemic toxicity. Calcium carbonate is potent but Ca2+ stimulates parietal cells and gastrin, causing acid rebound; with milk or bicarbonate it can cause milk-alkali syndrome.

cards.front: A patient has heartburn: how do you choose between antacid, H2 blocker and PPI, and why not antacids for an ulcer?
cards.back: Occasional heartburn or mild stage-1 GERD: on-demand antacid (fastest relief but no lasting benefit) or an H2 blocker. Persistent or erosive GERD: a PPI, usually in a higher or twice-daily dose, because it suppresses acid most completely. Antacids are not used to heal ulcers: they need large frequent doses, cause rebound and bowel upset, give little nocturnal cover and are poorly accepted. Stagger antacids from tetracyclines, iron and quinolones by 2 h.

cards.front: Where is the chemoreceptor trigger zone, and why can blood-borne drugs act on it?
cards.back: In the area postrema, which lies outside the blood-brain barrier, so circulating drugs, toxins and hormones can act on it directly. It relays signals to the nucleus tractus solitarius, which drives the vomiting centre in the medulla.

cards.front: How do cytotoxic drugs and radiation trigger vomiting through serotonin?
cards.back: Gut cell damage releases 5-HT from enterochromaffin cells. It activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents, which carry the signal to the nucleus tractus solitarius and the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Substance P acting on NK1 receptors adds to the signal.

cards.front: Which antiemetic class is first choice for motion sickness, and when should it be taken?
cards.back: Drugs with anticholinergic and antihistaminic action: hyoscine (the most effective, but short acting, so suited to short journeys) and H1 antihistamines such as promethazine, dimenhydrinate and meclozine. They work best when taken about 1 hour before the journey. Dopamine blockers and 5-HT3 antagonists are less effective.

cards.front: Classify: dopamine-blocking antiemetics
cards.text: Phenothiazines such as {{prochlorperazine}} and butyrophenones such as {{haloperidol}} block {{D2}} receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

cards.front: Classify: CINV drugs
cards.text: The NK1 antagonist {{aprepitant}} blocks the action of {{substance P}}, while the 5-HT3 antagonist {{ondansetron}} blocks {{5-HT}} signals on vagal afferents.

cards.front: What is an effective IV ondansetron schedule for highly emetogenic cisplatin?
cards.back: KDT: 8 mg IV given slowly over about 15 minutes, starting about 30 minutes before the cisplatin infusion, then two more 8 mg doses 4 hours apart; a single 24 mg dose on day 1 has also been used, and 8 mg orally twice daily for 3 to 5 days for delayed vomiting. GG14 gives the adult dose as 8 to 16 mg IV or 16 to 24 mg orally. Ondansetron alone is weak against delayed vomiting, so it is combined with dexamethasone and an NK1 antagonist.

cards.front: Why is palonosetron preferred for delayed chemotherapy-induced vomiting?
cards.back: It has the highest 5-HT3 receptor affinity and the longest half-life in its class (about 40 hours), so it controls delayed vomiting (days 2 to 5) better than ondansetron and keeps its efficacy in repeat cycles. Dose: 250 microgram (0.25 mg) by slow IV injection 30 minutes before chemotherapy, not repeated within 7 days. GG14 notes that, unlike first-generation 5-HT3 antagonists, it does not appear to prolong the QT interval.

cards.front: What does aprepitant add to a standard antiemetic regimen, and what are its key interactions?
cards.back: It is a selective NK1 antagonist that blocks substance P in the brain. Added to ondansetron and dexamethasone for cisplatin, it mainly improves protection against delayed vomiting. It is metabolised by CYP3A4, so it can raise dexamethasone levels and alter warfarin effect, and those doses need adjusting.

cards.front: Short note: Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV)

points: Chemotherapy releases 5-HT from gut cells; substance P acts on NK1 receptors in the brain
Acute phase (first 24 hours) and delayed phase (days 2 to 5)
NK1 antagonist (aprepitant, fosaprepitant, rolapitant) + 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone, or netupitant-palonosetron + dexamethasone
Delayed phase: dexamethasone, with aprepitant on days 2 and 3; olanzapine is another option
Granisetron: about 10 times more potent, half-life 8 to 12 hours
Palonosetron: best for delayed vomiting
Dexamethasone: improves acute and delayed control
Benzodiazepines: relieve anticipatory vomiting
Dronabinol: for resistant cases; central effects limit use
Headache, constipation or diarrhoea, dizziness with 5-HT3 antagonists
QT prolongation with first-generation 5-HT3 antagonists; palonosetron does not appear to prolong QT
Serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs

cards.front: Short note: Antiemetics for motion sickness and postoperative vomiting

points: Vestibular input reaches the vomiting centre through the cerebellum, using muscarinic and H1 pathways
Anticholinergic antihistamines: hyoscine, promethazine, diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate, meclozine
Cinnarizine: blocks calcium entry into vestibular cells
Phenothiazines and butyrophenones: less effective in motion sickness
5-HT3 antagonists: good for postoperative vomiting, poor for motion sickness
Hyoscine transdermal patch, behind the ear, releases over 3 days
Meclozine lasts about 24 hours with less sedation
Ondansetron is preferred; metoclopramide, dexamethasone and a single aprepitant dose are alternatives
Sedation: avoid driving
Neuroleptics: diagnose the cause first so that obstruction or appendicitis is not masked

cards.front: Essay: Management of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting

points: Gut release of 5-HT acting on vagal afferents
Central substance P and dopamine D2 pathways
Acute and delayed phases
Highly emetogenic (e.g. cisplatin): NK1 antagonist + 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone
Moderately emetogenic: 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone, with an NK1 antagonist, or olanzapine + palonosetron + dexamethasone
Low risk: dexamethasone, metoclopramide or prochlorperazine
Benzodiazepines for anticipatory vomiting
Cannabinoids for resistant cases
Metoclopramide or prochlorperazine as rescue, with antidystonic cover
Constipation and headache with 5-HT3 antagonists; QT prolongation with first-generation agents
Dystonia and sedation with dopamine blockers
Assess the response and adjust the regimen in later cycles

cards.front: Which receptors does metoclopramide use in the gut to speed gastric emptying?
cards.back: It is a 5-HT4 agonist on myenteric neurones, which increases acetylcholine release and so improves propulsive contraction and lower oesophageal sphincter tone. Its D2 blockade in the gut and weak 5-HT3 block add to this at higher doses. Atropine blocks the 5-HT4 effect.

cards.front: Metoclopramide: receptor actions
cards.text: Metoclopramide acts as a {{5-HT4}} agonist in the gut and as a {{D2}} antagonist in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

cards.front: Ursodiol and gallstones
cards.text: Ursodiol dissolves small cholesterol gallstones by {{lowering}} the cholesterol content of bile; its plasma half-life is about {{4 days}} because of enterohepatic cycling.

cards.front: What are the adverse effects of metoclopramide, and which are most important in children?
cards.back: Sedation, dizziness, loose stools and extrapyramidal effects: acute dystonias (more common in children and young adults, often after IV use and possibly after a single dose) and parkinsonism after weeks of use. Tardive dyskinesia can follow chronic use and may be irreversible. Hyperprolactinaemia causes galactorrhoea and gynaecomastia; QT prolongation and methaemoglobinaemia in neonates are also reported.

cards.front: How does domperidone differ from metoclopramide?
cards.back: Domperidone is a D2 antagonist that barely crosses the blood-brain barrier, so extrapyramidal effects are rare and it does not oppose levodopa in Parkinson disease. Its prokinetic action is not reversed by atropine. It still acts on brain areas outside the barrier: the chemoreceptor trigger zone (antiemetic) and prolactin control (galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia). It carries a risk of serious ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death, especially above 60 years and at doses over 30 mg/day.

cards.front: Why was cisapride withdrawn from most markets?
cards.back: It blocks cardiac delayed-rectifier potassium channels, which prolongs the QT interval and risks torsades de pointes. The risk rises with CYP3A4 inhibitors such as azole antifungals and macrolides. It was banned in India in 2011.

cards.front: Short note: Metoclopramide

points: Substituted benzamide; antiemetic and gastrokinetic
5-HT4 agonist in the gut; D2 antagonist in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
Weak 5-HT3 blockade at high doses
Postoperative, drug-induced and migraine-associated vomiting
Adjunct to ondansetron or dexamethasone in cisplatin chemotherapy
Emptying the stomach before emergency anaesthesia; diabetic or postvagotomy gastroparesis
Hiccups; mild GERD (less effective than PPIs)
Oral onset within about 1 hour, IV within minutes; action lasts 4 to 6 hours
Half-life 3 to 6 hours; excreted in urine
Sedation, dystonia (children), parkinsonism with long use, hyperprolactinaemia
Blocks the action of levodopa; alters absorption of aspirin, diazepam and digoxin

cards.front: Short note: Prokinetic drugs, classes and safety

points: Drugs that speed coordinated gut propulsion, unlike cholinomimetics that cause tonic contraction
D2 antagonists: metoclopramide, domperidone, levosulpiride
5-HT4 agonists: cisapride, mosapride, prucalopride
Itopride: D2 blocker with anticholinesterase activity
Cinitapride: 5-HT4 agonist that also blocks D2 and 5-HT2
Cisapride: QT prolongation and torsades; CYP3A4 inhibitors raise the risk
Mosapride: later reports of QT prolongation
Itopride: not metabolised by CYP enzymes, so no CYP3A4 interaction
Functional dyspepsia, diabetic gastroparesis, GERD as an adjunct to PPIs
Efficacy often modest; PPIs are better for reflux

cards.front: Essay: Prokinetic drugs and their place in gastrointestinal disorders

points: Coordinated propulsion rather than tonic contraction
Effects on gastric emptying and LES tone
Metoclopramide: central and peripheral action; extrapyramidal effects and prolactin rise
Domperidone: peripheral; fewer CNS effects; arrhythmia on rapid IV injection
Cisapride: effective, but withdrawn for QT prolongation and arrhythmia
Mosapride: 5-HT4 agonist with minor 5-HT3 block; no extrapyramidal effects; later reports of QT prolongation with CYP3A4 inhibitors
Gastroparesis, functional dyspepsia, adjunct in GERD
Prokinetics do not heal oesophagitis and are inferior to PPIs
Check interacting drugs and QT-prolonging co-medication
Use for symptom control with a clear review point

cards.front: Why must bulk-forming laxatives be taken with plenty of water, and what do they not do?
cards.back: They swell by absorbing water, which softens stool and speeds transit. Without enough fluid they can cause impaction, and ispaghula must never be swallowed dry. They take several days for full effect and do not soften stool already in the rectum, so they prevent constipation rather than treat it.

cards.front: Short note: Classification of laxatives

points: Laxative: soft formed stool; purgative: stronger, more fluid evacuation
Ispaghula, methylcellulose, bran: water-holding, fermentable fibre
Docusate: anionic detergent that draws water into stool
Liquid paraffin: lubricant; avoid regular use (granulomas, lipid pneumonia, fat-soluble vitamin loss)
Bisacodyl and sodium picosulfate: act on colonic mucosa and enteric neurones
Senna and cascara: anthraquinone glycosides activated by colonic bacteria; act in 6 to 8 hours
Magnesium and sodium salts: bowel preparation, poisoning, tapeworm clearance
Lactulose and lactitol: fermented to acidic osmotic products
Prucalopride (5-HT4 agonist), lubiprostone (chloride channel activator)

cards.front: How does dietary fibre or ispaghula relieve constipation, and what are its limits?
cards.back: It absorbs water, swells and softens stool, adds bacterial mass by fermentation and speeds colonic transit. Take with plenty of water; ispaghula is never swallowed dry (oesophageal impaction). Acts in 1 to 3 days; it prevents constipation but does not soften stool already in the rectum. Avoid with ulceration, stenosis or impaction risk; bran may worsen IBS.

cards.front: How do stimulant purgatives (bisacodyl, senna) produce their effect?
cards.back: They accumulate water and electrolytes in the lumen by inhibiting Na+K+ATPase in villous cells and raising cAMP and prostaglandins in crypt cells, and also excite myenteric neurones. Bisacodyl is deacetylated in the gut; senna glycosides are freed by colonic bacteria, so bedtime doses act after 6 to 8 h. Overuse causes hypokalaemia and colonic atony.

cards.front: Why are stimulant laxatives such as bisacodyl and senna contraindicated in pregnancy and in bowel obstruction?
cards.back: They can stimulate the gravid uterus reflexly, and they increase propulsion and fluid secretion, which is dangerous with an obstruction. Regular use causes hypokalaemia and colonic atony, and senna can cause melanosis of the colon.

cards.front: How does lactulose lower blood ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.back: Colonic bacteria break lactulose down into acidic, osmotically active products. The lower stool pH turns ammonia into the ionised, non-absorbable ammonium form, and the laxative effect clears it. Blood ammonia can fall by 25 to 50 percent. Lactitol works similarly.

cards.front: What are prucalopride and lubiprostone, and what is the key safety point for each?
cards.back: Prucalopride is a 5-HT4 agonist that boosts colonic propulsion. It is used for chronic constipation in women when other laxatives fail, and appears to lack the cardiovascular risk that ended tegaserod. Lubiprostone is a prostaglandin analogue that opens chloride channels to draw fluid into the gut; nausea is its commonest side effect, and it is reserved for patients who have failed at least two other laxative classes.

cards.front: Short note: Constipation, rational treatment and purgative abuse

points: A symptom: infrequent hard stool, straining or incomplete evacuation
Normal frequency varies from once every 2 days to 3 times daily
Functional: spastic (hard stool, irritable bowel) or atonic (age, debility, laxative abuse)
Secondary: obstruction, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, opioids, anticholinergics, oral iron, clonidine, verapamil
Diet, fluids, exercise and regular habits first
Spastic: soluble fibre; atonic: bulk or osmotic agent; stimulants last
Enema preferred to treat impaction
Keep stool soft in hernia, cardiovascular disease and perianal surgery
Bowel preparation: saline purgative, bisacodyl or senna
Hypokalaemia, steatorrhoea, protein-losing enteropathy, spastic colitis

cards.front: Choose a laxative for each: pregnancy, avoiding straining, colonoscopy preparation, hepatic encephalopathy, impaction. Justify.
cards.back: Pregnancy: bulk or osmotic agents, since stimulants can reflexly stimulate the gravid uterus. Avoid straining (hernia, cardiac disease, perianal surgery): bran or docusate to keep stool soft. Colonoscopy: saline purgative such as magnesium citrate with sodium picosulfate, or bisacodyl or senna. Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose, whose acidic products trap ammonia. Impaction: an enema, not bran. Never use liquid paraffin routinely (granulomas, lipid pneumonia, vitamin loss).

cards.front: What are the components and total osmolarity of the WHO low-osmolarity oral rehydration solution?
cards.back: Sodium 75 mmol/L, glucose 75 mmol/L, potassium 20 mmol/L, chloride 65 mmol/L and citrate 10 mmol/L, with a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L. The older standard formula (310 mOsm/L, higher sodium) caused periorbital oedema in children and produced more stool and vomiting.

cards.front: What is the role of zinc in acute childhood diarrhoea, and how is it given?
cards.back: Given with low-osmolarity ORS, zinc shortens and reduces the severity of the episode and lowers recurrence for 2 to 3 months. It is given for 10 to 14 days: 20 mg per day for children aged 6 to 60 months and 10 mg per day under 6 months.

cards.front: Short note: Antidiarrhoeal drugs

points: Bulking colloids such as ispaghula; kaolin and pectin adsorbents are banned in India
Racecadotril: enkephalinase inhibitor
Bismuth subsalicylate: reduces prostaglandin-driven chloride secretion; used for travellers' diarrhoea
Octreotide: somatostatin analogue for carcinoid or VIP tumour diarrhoea; given subcutaneously
Loperamide: potent peripheral opioid, most suitable antimotility drug for adults
Diphenoxylate with atropine: CNS effects; contraindicated under 6 years
Codeine: not used for diarrhoea because of dependence
Avoid antimotility drugs in invasive diarrhoea, severe colitis and young children

cards.front: Diphenoxylate: classification and limits
cards.text: Diphenoxylate is a synthetic {{opioid}} given with {{atropine}} to discourage abuse, and it is contraindicated below {{6}} years of age.

cards.front: Why does loperamide cause few central effects, and when must it be avoided?
cards.back: It is a peripheral mu-opioid agonist (40 to 50 times as potent as morphine as an antidiarrhoeal) that is poorly absorbed and barely enters the brain, so at normal doses it has no analgesic action and little abuse liability. GG14 warns that exceeding the recommended dose can cause torsades de pointes, cardiac arrest and death. Avoid it in invasive diarrhoea (fever, blood or mucus; risk of toxic megacolon and systemic spread), in severe colitis, and in young children (KDT: under 4 years; GG14: not recommended under 2 years).

cards.front: How does racecadotril reduce diarrhoea without slowing the gut?
cards.back: It is a prodrug converted to thiorphan, an enkephalinase inhibitor. By protecting natural enkephalins it lowers mucosal cAMP and cuts intestinal secretion, but leaves motility alone. It is not contraindicated in children; the usual dose is 100 mg three times daily for up to 7 days.

cards.front: In acute diarrhoea, which features suggest an invasive cause that needs an antibiotic?
cards.back: Blood and mucus in the stool, fever, urgency and cramps, with only mild dehydration, point to colonic invasion (for example Shigella, EPEC, Campylobacter or Salmonella typhimurium). Watery diarrhoea with vomiting and little fever points to a noninvasive cause, where oral rehydration is the mainstay.

cards.front: Short note: Management of acute infectious diarrhoea

points: Rehydration first, then nutrition; drugs only when indicated
Most acute diarrhoea is self-limiting
Oral route for mild to moderate loss
IV if loss exceeds 10 percent of body weight, stool loss exceeds 10 ml per kg per hour, or oral intake is impossible
Ringer lactate or a sodium, potassium and bicarbonate solution as IV fluid
Do not starve; continue breast milk, rice, banana, soup and fruit juice
Noninvasive: no routine antibiotic
Invasive: ciprofloxacin or another fluoroquinolone, cotrimoxazole or doxycycline (KDT); fluoroquinolones are first line for traveller's diarrhoea in adults (GG14)
Cholera: tetracycline halves stool volume
C. difficile: stop the offending antibiotic; oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are now preferred, metronidazole only for nonsevere disease
Avoid antibiotics in enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (haemolytic uraemic syndrome)
Zinc in children; probiotics have weak evidence for routine use

cards.front: Sulfasalazine: how it works
cards.text: Colonic bacteria split the {{azo}} bond of sulfasalazine to release {{5-aminosalicylic acid}}, the active anti-inflammatory part, and {{sulfapyridine}}, which causes most side effects.

cards.front: Azathioprine: a dangerous genetic interaction
cards.text: Azathioprine is converted to {{6-mercaptopurine}}; patients deficient in the enzyme {{TPMT}} are at high risk of severe bone marrow toxicity.

cards.front: Short note: Prebiotics and probiotics in bowel disorders

points: Probiotics are live microbes such as lactobacilli, bifidobacteria and Saccharomyces boulardii
Prebiotics are poorly digested fibres or oligosaccharides that feed beneficial gut bacteria
Synbiotics combine both
Some strains shorten acute infectious diarrhoea in children
Saccharomyces boulardii and Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG reduce antibiotic-associated diarrhoea
Probiotics aid H. pylori eradication by improving response to antibiotics
Probiotics help prevent the first attack and relapse of pouchitis
E. coli Nissle may match mesalazine in maintaining remission of ulcerative colitis
No proven benefit for maintenance of remission in Crohn's disease
Lactulose, a prebiotic disaccharide, is used for constipation and hepatic encephalopathy
Probiotics are generally safe; caution in immunocompromised patients

cards.front: Essay: Drug therapy of inflammatory bowel disease

points: Ulcerative colitis: continuous mucosal disease of the colon, spreading up from the rectum
Crohn's disease: patchy transmural disease anywhere in the gut
Extraintestinal features in up to half of patients
Sulfasalazine: releases 5-ASA in the colon; sulfapyridine causes most side effects; give folic acid
Mesalazine, olsalazine, balsalazide: deliver 5-ASA to the colon with fewer side effects; 5-ASA not useful in Crohn's
Prednisolone to induce remission, then taper; not for long-term maintenance
Budesonide (delayed-release) targets ileal or colonic disease with fewer systemic effects
Azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine for steroid-dependent or resistant disease; check TPMT status
Methotrexate for severe Crohn's disease, given parenterally
Cyclosporine as a short bridge in severe ulcerative colitis
Anti-TNF: infliximab (closes fistulas; better with azathioprine) or adalimumab for moderate to severe disease
Vedolizumab: blocks lymphocyte homing to gut mucosa (MAdCAM-1 binding); Crohn disease and UC
Ustekinumab: anti-IL-12/IL-23 (p40); Crohn disease
Tofacitinib: oral JAK inhibitor

cards.front: Essay: Oral rehydration therapy in acute diarrhoea

points: Sodium absorption coupled to glucose by the sodium-glucose cotransporter survives in diarrhoea
Secreted fluid contains no glucose, so it cannot be reabsorbed
Isotonic or slightly hypotonic: osmolarity 200 to 310 mOsm/L
Glucose equal to or slightly above sodium, not above 110 mM
Potassium 15 to 25 mM and a base such as citrate 8 to 12 mM
WHO low-osmolarity formula: 245 mOsm/L; less stool output and vomiting than the older formula
Frequent drinks; replace stool losses; aim to restore hydration within about 6 hours
Nasogastric drip if a weak child refuses
ORS does not stop diarrhoea; zinc is added in children; food should not be withheld

cards.front: Magnesium hydroxide as an antacid: how strong is it?
cards.back: It reacts promptly with hydrochloric acid, so it is an efficacious antacid: about 1 g neutralises about 30 mEq of acid. Its suspension (milk of magnesia) is only weakly alkaline because the hydroxide is poorly soluble.

cards.front: Magnesium trisilicate: how much acid does it really neutralise?
cards.back: It is poorly soluble and slow to react. Although 1 g can react with about 10 mEq of acid, in clinical use only about 1 mEq is neutralised.

cards.front: Name the magnesium salts used as saline (osmotic) purgatives.
cards.back: Magnesium sulfate, magnesium citrate and milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide). They act osmotically, holding water in the bowel.

cards.front: Besides osmosis, how do magnesium ions produce their purgative action?
cards.back: They release cholecystokinin, which augments intestinal motility and secretion. All inorganic saline purgatives act this way and differ only in dose, palatability and the risk of systemic toxicity.

cards.front: Magnesium sulfate in pre-eclampsia: what does it treat, and by what route?
cards.back: It is the first-line i.v. drug for preventing and treating seizures in pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. It also acts as a tocolytic by competing with Ca2+ entry into myometrium, but its use to delay premature labour is risky and not recommended.

cards.front: Magnesium sulfate in acute severe asthma: what role does it play?
cards.back: It is useful as an additional bronchodilator in children and adults with acute severe asthma, given on top of the standard bronchodilators.

cards.front: Short note: Therapeutic uses of magnesium

points: Magnesium hydroxide: prompt, strong acid neutraliser (about 1 g per 30 mEq); milk of magnesia
Magnesium trisilicate: poorly soluble, only about 1 mEq neutralised in clinical use
Magnesium sulfate, magnesium citrate and milk of magnesia
Acts osmotically and by releasing cholecystokinin, which increases motility and secretion
Saline purgatives differ only in dose, palatability and risk of systemic toxicity
First-line i.v. drug for seizures in pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
Tocolytic action, but not recommended for delaying preterm labour
Additional bronchodilator in acute severe asthma, children and adults

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacotherapy of irritable bowel syndrome

points: Visceral hypersensitivity plus altered motility; constipation, diarrhoea or both
Serotonin involved in sensitisation and motility, which guides newer drugs
Treatment is mainly symptomatic
Soluble ispaghula taken over weeks eases pain, constipation and diarrhoea
Insoluble bran can worsen symptoms
Diet limits (FODMAPs, lactose, gluten) help some patients
Dicyclomine and hyoscyamine (muscarinic); glycopyrrolate and methscopolamine cause fewer CNS effects
Mebeverine acts directly on smooth muscle; used outside the US
Dicyclomine 20 mg every 6 h, increasing to 40 mg every 6 h unless limited by side effects
Alosetron (5-HT3 antagonist) for severe IBS-D in women, under restricted distribution
Eluxadoline (opioid receptor profile) with biliary and pancreatic cautions
Rifaximin (550 mg three times daily for 2 weeks)
Ispaghula first; stimulant purgatives contraindicated
Prucalopride (5-HT4 agonist) and lubiprostone (PG analogue)
Low-dose tricyclic antidepressant for visceral pain, independent of its antidepressant effect
SSRIs can increase bowel movements or cause diarrhoea, and are probably less effective for visceral pain

cards.front: Alosetron: what is it, and why is it restricted?
cards.back: A 5-HT3 antagonist for severe diarrhoea-predominant IBS in women. It was withdrawn for ischaemic colitis, then re-approved under a limited distribution system.

cards.front: Eluxadoline: receptor profile and main contraindication.
cards.back: Mixed mu-opioid agonist, delta-opioid antagonist and kappa-opioid agonist, which eases pain and diarrhoea in IBS. Avoid with sphincter of Oddi spasm or pancreatitis.

cards.front: Why are low-dose tricyclic antidepressants used in IBS?
cards.back: They have neuromodulatory and analgesic effects that reduce visceral pain, separate from their antidepressant action. Amitriptyline, nortriptyline or imipramine are used off-label, with a track record in functional visceral pain.

cards.front: Rifaximin in IBS: which subtype, and what dose?
cards.back: Diarrhoea-predominant IBS: 550 mg three times daily for 2 weeks, re-treated up to twice if symptoms recur. It is minimally absorbed, so it acts mainly in the gut.

cards.front: Why are glycopyrrolate and methscopolamine preferred over dicyclomine in IBS?
cards.back: They cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, so they carry a lower risk of neurological effects such as drowsiness and light-headedness.

cards.front: Mebeverine: class, mechanism and use?
cards.back: A hydroxybenzamide derivative used outside the US as an antispasmodic in IBS. It acts directly on smooth muscle by blocking K+, Na+ and Ca2+ channels.

cards.front: Why is bran a poor choice for IBS, while ispaghula helps?
cards.back: Insoluble fibres such as bran can worsen IBS symptoms. Soluble ispaghula, used over weeks, reduces rectosigmoid pressure and eases pain, constipation and diarrhoea.

cards.front: What is the gut microbiome, and how does it compare with the human host?
cards.back: The genetic repertoire of the microbes (mainly bacteria, plus viruses, archaea and fungi) living in the gut. It carries over 200 million genes against about 20,000 human genes, and microbial cells are roughly equal in number to human cells.

cards.front: Sulfasalazine: which bacterial reaction releases the active drug?
cards.back: Gut bacteria reduce the azo bond, releasing 5-aminosalicylate (mesalamine), the active part, and sulfapyridine.

cards.front: Digoxin: which gut bacterium inactivates it, and how?
cards.back: Eggerthella lenta reduces the lactone ring of digoxin to form dihydrodigoxin, an inactive metabolite. A high-arginine diet inhibits this reduction.

cards.front: How does the gut microbiome prolong a drug's half-life through enterohepatic recycling?
cards.back: The liver excretes conjugated drug (glucuronides, sulfates) in bile. Gut microbes hydrolyse the conjugates back to the more lipophilic parent, which is reabsorbed into the portal blood. This cycle prolongs elimination.

cards.front: Irinotecan: why do gut bacteria matter for its diarrhoea?
cards.back: The liver converts irinotecan to SN-38 and UGT1A1 glucuronidates it. The inactive glucuronide is secreted in bile, and bacterial beta-glucuronidases in the gut remove the glucuronide, releasing active SN-38. High intestinal SN-38 causes the dose-limiting severe diarrhoea.

cards.front: How can antibiotics change drug response through the microbiome?
cards.back: Antibiotics change the composition of gut microbes, which can alter how drugs are handled. Many non-antibiotic drugs also inhibit some gut bacteria in vitro (240 drugs in one study).

cards.front: Which microbiome-based therapy treats recurrent C. difficile colitis?
cards.back: Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), which reshapes the patient's gut microbiome to resemble that of a healthy donor.

cards.front: What is the evidence for probiotics in diarrhoea, and what caution applies?
cards.back: Live or freeze-dried microbes (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Saccharomyces boulardii) help antibiotic-associated, C. difficile and acute infective diarrhoea, and reduce traveller's diarrhoea. Evidence is not yet convincing enough for standard use.

cards.front: How does diet change drug response through the microbiome?
cards.back: A high-arginine diet inhibits the bacterial reduction of digoxin.

cards.front: Short note: Impact of the human gut microbiome on therapeutics

points: Genetic repertoire of gut bacteria, viruses and some archaea and fungi
Over 200 million microbial genes against about 20,000 human genes
Sulfasalazine azo reduction releases mesalamine
Eggerthella lenta reduces digoxin to an inactive metabolite
Bacterial beta-glucuronidase reactivates irinotecan's SN-38 in the gut
Deconjugation drives enterohepatic recycling and prolongs half-life
Antibiotics change gut microbial composition, altering drug response
Many non-antibiotic drugs inhibit some gut bacteria in vitro
FMT for recurrent C. difficile colitis
Probiotics help antibiotic-associated and infectious diarrhoea, but evidence is not yet convincing for standard use
Diet shapes the microbiome; a high-arginine diet blocks digoxin reduction
Microbiome differences between patients favour individualised therapy
